title: Is Jesus the Only Way?
excerpt: The claim that Jesus is the only way to God has been called arrogant since the second century. Read where it was first spoken, it is narrower and stranger than the slogan, and every alternative to it also tells most of the world that it is wrong.
body:
A nurse has worked nights for eleven years beside a woman who keeps the five daily prayers of Islam and who has sat with more dying patients than anyone else on the ward. A father is about to gain a son-in-law whose Hindu parents have shown his daughter more plain kindness than some people in his own church ever did. A graduate student who grew up in Sunday school can name the week he stopped going. It was the week a teacher explained, cheerfully, that everyone outside the faith was wrong.

Each of them has run into the same sentence. Christians say that Jesus is the only way to God. The nurse wonders whether she is required to believe something terrible about her friend. The father wonders what he is supposed to say at the wedding. The student thinks it is the most arrogant thing a religion has ever said, and he wonders how anyone who has met the neighbors can go on saying it.

## The Charge

The student's objection is a moral one, and it should be heard at full strength. The scholar of religion Wilfred Cantwell Smith put it into a single sentence in 1976. As the page on this site that weighs [the charge of arrogance](/questions/religions/is-it-arrogant-to-say-jesus-is-the-only-way) quotes him, "except at the cost of insensitivity or delinquency, it is morally not possible actually to go out into the world and say to devout, intelligent fellow human beings [that] we believe that we know God and we are right; you believe that you know God, and you are totally wrong."

The facts behind that sentence are not in dispute. Most of the human beings who have ever lived were not Christians. A person's faith usually follows the map, and nobody chooses a birthplace. Other faiths have produced people whose patience and mercy would shame most churchgoers. And the sentence has a record. It has traveled with armies.

## An Old Complaint

The objection sounds modern. It is as old as the church.

Celsus, a pagan philosopher of the second century, left a long attack on Christianity. It survives in the passages the Christian teacher Origen quoted in order to answer it. One of his complaints was that Jews and Christians behaved as though their God were not everyone's. "It makes no difference," he wrote, "whether you call the highest being Zeus, or Zen, or Adonai, or Sabaoth, or Ammoun like the Egyptians, or Pappaeus like the Scythians." Rome had room for every god except one that would not share a shelf.

The stubbornness was inherited. Israel had been saying it for centuries: "I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God" (Isaiah 45:5). The narrowness that annoyed Celsus in the church was the narrowness he already disliked in the synagogue.

The most graceful statement of the complaint came two hundred years later, and by then the positions had been reversed. In 384 the senator Symmachus wrote to a Christian emperor on behalf of the Roman Senate, asking that the altar of the goddess Victory be set up again in the Senate house. "We look on the same stars, the sky is common, the same world surrounds us," he wrote. "What difference does it make by what pains each seeks the truth? We cannot attain to so great a secret by one road."

When Peter first said there was no other name, he was a prisoner. When Symmachus asked for many roads, he was the petitioner and the Christians had the emperor's ear. The claim had not changed between those two rooms. The people making it had gained the power to hurt, and most of the trouble in this subject starts there.

## What Should Be Granted

The history is as bad as the student thinks. This site's course on church history tells how Charlemagne spent thirty years subduing the pagan Saxons. Under the law he gave them a man could be put to death for declining baptism, and his own court's annals record the beheading of thousands of prisoners on one day in 782. We did that, in the name on which Peter said salvation rests, and a good deal like it afterward. No reading of the New Testament makes it faithful.

And the goodness of people outside the church is something the New Testament points at more often than Christians do. When Jesus wanted a picture of love for a neighbor, he chose a Samaritan, a man of the wrong religion, and had him do what a priest and a Levite would not: "when he saw him, he had compassion" (Luke 10:33). In his hometown synagogue he reminded the congregation that in a land full of lepers the one healed was "Naaman the Syrian" (Luke 4:27), and they tried to throw him off a cliff. Of a Roman officer he said, "not even in Israel have I found such faith" (Luke 7:9).

Nor does the Christian claim require that other peoples know nothing of God. Paul told a pagan crowd that God "did not leave himself without witness" among them (Acts 14:17). John's Gospel opens by calling Christ "the true light, which gives light to everyone" (John 1:9). Whatever the claim means, it cannot mean that truth and goodness stop at the church door, because the church's own book says they don't.

## The Two Sentences

The sentence the student objects to was first spoken in a private room, to a handful of frightened friends, on the night of the arrest. Jesus had told them he was going away. He had said, "In my Father's house are many rooms" (John 14:2). Thomas said what the rest were thinking: "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" (John 14:5). The famous line is the reply to that question. "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). A moment later Philip asked to be shown the Father, and was told, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9).

Read where it stands, the sentence is about Jesus and says almost nothing about anyone else. The Study Bible's note on John 14 observes that he "does not say he knows the way or teaches the way, but that he is the way." The claim is that the God of Israel can be seen and reached in this one man, because of who the man is. That is an enormous thing for anyone to say. But it does not grade the world's religions or rank its peoples, and it does not say what the Father will do with a person who never had the chance to hear it, a question that has [an essay of its own](/writing/what-happens-to-people-who-never-hear-the-gospel) on this site.

The second sentence is Peter's. He and John had healed a man who had been unable to walk since birth. They were arrested, and after a night in custody the council in Jerusalem asked them, "By what power or by what name did you do this?" (Acts 4:7). Peter's answer ends, "there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). Ordered to be quiet, the two replied, "we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard" (Acts 4:20).

Three things in that scene are easy to miss. Everyone in the room was Jewish, so nobody was looking down on a foreign religion. It was an argument inside Israel about what Israel's God had just done. The speaker had no power at all, as the Study Bible's note on Acts 4 has it: "Peter is not a powerful man imposing his religion on the weak; he is a prisoner on trial before the powerful." And the reason he gives for speaking is that he saw something. He does not claim a better philosophy. His case rests on an event, the man "whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead" (Acts 4:10).

So the claim as its first speakers made it is narrower and stranger than the slogan. It says that God has done one particular thing for the whole world through one particular man, and that no second rescue is running alongside it. Paul states it in a way that leaves no room for pride: "by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Ephesians 2:8–9). A Christian who is proud of being on the right road has forgotten what he says he believes about how he got there.

## Three Answers

Three names are commonly used for the answers people give. Each stands for a position that serious people hold.

The first is called exclusivism. It holds that Jesus is the one Savior and that his rescue is received by trusting him. The Heidelberg Catechism of 1563 asks why the Son of God is called Jesus, a name that means Savior, and answers: "Because He saves us from all our sins, and because salvation is not to be sought or found in anyone else." People who hold this are not saying that they are better than their neighbors. They are saying that everyone is in the same trouble, themselves first, and that there turned out to be one door. In its strict form the view holds that a person must hear of Christ and believe in this life. It points to the urgency of the New Testament, whose apostles preached to devout people and did not tell them they were fine as they were.

The second is called inclusivism. It agrees entirely that Christ alone saves. It holds that his rescue may reach further than the news of it has traveled, and that the God who "desires all people to be saved" (1 Timothy 2:4) may save through Christ some who never knew his name but answered the light they were given. The site's page on [those who never heard](/questions/religions/those-who-never-heard) records that the Second Vatican Council taught in 1964 that people who do not know the gospel through no fault of their own, and who seek God sincerely, may be saved. Inclusivists point to Abraham, who was saved by a Christ he never heard named, and to what Peter said at the door of a Roman officer: "in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him" (Acts 10:35). On this view the other religions are not ways of salvation. Christ is, and he is freer than his messengers.

The third is pluralism, and its most careful defender was the philosopher John Hick. In his account, as the site's page on [whether the religions are all the same](/questions/religions/are-all-religions-the-same) sets it out, there is one ultimate reality beyond every human description, and the great faiths are different responses to it, each formed by a culture. He never said they teach the same things. He said that each "constitutes a valid context of salvation/liberation; but none constitutes the one and only such context." His chief evidence was that the great traditions, as far as anyone can observe, turn people away from self-centeredness about equally well. Pluralists believe that God, or the Real, is greater than any tradition's account, and that humility requires saying so.

## What Each Has to Explain

It is a fair test of a view to see what it does with its own worst difficulty.

The strict exclusivist has to answer the student. If a person must hear and believe, a child's eternal future seems to turn on where she was born, and that sits badly beside a God who "shows no partiality" (Acts 10:34). The usual reply is that no one is condemned for failing to hear, only for sin, and that God can bring the news to anyone who seeks him. Many who give that reply admit that the ache remains.

The inclusivist has to answer the New Testament. If God saves people who have never heard, it is hard to see why the apostles spent their lives the way they did, or why devout people in the book of Acts are told about Jesus when they might simply have been congratulated. And to tell a faithful Muslim that Christ may be saving her without her knowledge is, from where she stands, its own kind of condescension. She has not asked to be counted as a Christian in disguise.

The pluralist has to explain the contradictions. Christians confess that Jesus was crucified and raised. The Qur'an, in the translation the site's page quotes, says that "they slew him not nor crucified him, but it appeared so unto them." Jewish teaching is still waiting for the Messiah. These are three answers to a question of fact, and they cannot all be correct. Hick knew it, and his solution was that none of them is literally true. They are true, he held, in the sense that they change lives. But that tells the Muslim she is mistaken about the Qur'an and the Christian that he is mistaken about Easter. The Hindu devoted to a personal Lord is told the same. Pluralism turns out to hold that every religion is wrong about the thing it cares for most, and that the pluralist can see, from no tradition in particular, what all of them missed. That is one more claim that most of the human race has God wrong, and most people who pray, in any tradition, would not recognize their own faith in it.

As far as logic can answer the charge of arrogance, that answers it. Every position on offer, the student's included, holds that billions of people, praying in good faith, have the largest question wrong. If that is arrogance, there is no humble seat in the room. So arrogance must be something else. It is contempt, and ignorance, and force.

## Respect Without Pretending

There is a cheap kind of respect that works by declining to listen. It tells the Muslim, the Jew and the Christian that deep down they all mean the same thing, which most of them would deny with some heat. The nurse's friend believes that God is one and has no son. Respecting her starts with believing that she means it.

The better kind is harder. It means learning what a neighbor believes well enough to say it back in words she would accept, granting what is true and admirable in it, saying plainly where you differ, and never using anything but words.

The New Testament asks for exactly that combination. The same Peter who said "no other name" told Christians to be ready with a reason for their hope, "yet do it with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:15). When a Samaritan village refused Jesus a night's lodging and two disciples offered to call down fire, "he turned and rebuked them" (Luke 9:55), and they walked on to the next village. Paul began in Athens with a compliment, "I perceive that in every way you are very religious" (Acts 17:22), and went on to tell them about a man raised from the dead. Some of them laughed.

The father at the wedding can honor his new family, eat at their table, learn what their prayers mean and love them without reserve. What he can't honestly do is tell them that he thinks nothing is at stake. They would probably think less of him if he did, since they don't think that either.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess, with the creeds, that there is one God, that his Son became man "for our salvation," was crucified and was raised, and that salvation is his gift and comes through him alone. The short [answer to this question](/answers/is-jesus-the-only-way) on this site says so in plain terms. That confession excludes pluralism. A faith in which Jesus is one teacher among several is a different faith from the one the apostles preached.

Whether Christ saves only those who hear and believe in this life, or also some who never heard, is a question on which churches that share the creeds differ. No creed decides it, and this essay does not.

Whether the confession is true cannot be settled by asking which view sounds kindest. Peter's claim rested on something he said had happened. If Jesus was not raised, Paul wrote, "your faith is futile and you are still in your sins" (1 Corinthians 15:17), and the student is right to stay away. If he was, then the sentence in John 14 was spoken by someone with the standing to say it. That is a question about history, and it is weighed in [the essay on the resurrection](/writing/did-the-resurrection-happen).

The nurse is not required to believe anything terrible about her friend. She is told nothing about what God will do with any one person, and she is not permitted to guess. She is asked to believe something about Jesus, and to be the kind of colleague whose belief is hard to hold against her. The student is owed an apology for the cheerfulness. Whoever taught him that week had mistaken a gift for an achievement.

The sentence is still there after the apology. It was first spoken by a man a few hours from his own execution, to a friend who had just admitted he was lost. It says that the Father has a face, and that this is the face. Symmachus was right that the secret is great, too great to be reached by one road or by a thousand. The Christian claim is that it did not wait to be reached.

*"Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?"* (John 14:5)

*"Whoever has seen me has seen the Father."* (John 14:9)
